provenance.accuracy: Jupiter position was compared with JPL Horizons (DE441) at six dates from 1969 to 2030: at most 1269 km (0.33 arcsec) from Horizons. Sample maxima, not a bound for every date.
provenance.notes: Geometric position about the Sun's centre; no light-time or aberration.

knownLimitations: Jupiter is drawn flat in one colour, without cloud bands: Planetary Explorer's Jupiter map has no recorded source or licence, so no texture is used.
The surface drawn is the 1-bar cloud-top level, not a solid surface.
The rings are drawn as flat bands in Planetary Explorer's colours; their brightness is a look, not a measurement.

panels.title: The most volcanic world we know
body: Io is only a little bigger than our Moon, yet it has hundreds of volcanoes, more than anywhere else in the solar system. Some throw fountains of lava high above the ground.
In late 1999 the Galileo spacecraft flew past Io and caught one of those fountains erupting.
details: NASA: Io is "the most volcanically active world in the solar system", with hundreds of volcanoes, some erupting lava fountains dozens of kilometres high.
Io's mean radius is 1,821.5 km; the Moon's is 1,737.4 km (NASA fact sheets).
Galileo, in orbit around Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, caught an eruption at Tvashtar Catena on 25 November 1999, with lava fountains up to 1.5 km above the surface (NASA Photojournal PIA02545).
The scene draws Io where NASA JPL's Horizons system places it; it shows no volcanoes or eruptions. This moment is chosen near the start of the scene so the first panel opens soon after play.
sources: NASA Science, Io: "the most volcanically active world in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes, some erupting lava fountains dozens of miles (or kilometers) high"; "only slightly larger than Earth's Moon"; https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/jupiter-moons/io/ (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Jovian Satellite Fact Sheet: Io mean radius 1821.5 km; https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/joviansatfact.html; Moon Fact Sheet: volumetric mean radius 1737.4 km; https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA Photojournal PIA02545, Eruption at Tvashtar Catena, Io, in Color: Galileo caught the eruption on 25 November 1999; fountains up to 1.5 km; https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/eruption-at-tvashtar-catena-io-in-color (accessed 2026-10-18)
NASA Science, Galileo mission: entered orbit on 7 December 1995, mission ended 21 September 2003; https://science.nasa.gov/mission/galileo/ (accessed 2026-10-18)

panels.title: Squeezed by a giant
body: Io's path around Jupiter is not quite a circle, so the giant planet's pull on it keeps changing. Io is squeezed and relaxed again and again, like a stress ball in a restless hand, and the squeezing heats it from inside.
Scientists worked this out in 1979 and predicted volcanoes, just days before the Voyager 1 spacecraft saw them erupting.
details: Io's orbital eccentricity is about 0.004 (NASA fact sheet). NASA describes Io as "caught in a tug-of-war" between Jupiter's gravity and the smaller, precisely timed pulls of Europa and Ganymede, which keep its orbit from becoming circular.

Peale, Cassen and Reynolds published the prediction in Science on 2 March 1979. Voyager 1 passed Io three days later, and navigation engineer Linda Morabito found the first volcanic plume in its images four days after the encounter (Morabito 2012).
Tidal heating is the accepted model of what powers Io's volcanoes, hence the modelled badge. The stress-ball comparison is a picture, not a measurement.
This moment is chosen for pacing; nothing special happens at this time.
sources: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Jovian Satellite Fact Sheet: Io eccentricity 0.004, orbital period 1.769138 days; https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/joviansatfact.html (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA Science, Io: "caught in a tug-of-war between Jupiter's massive gravity and the smaller but precisely timed pulls" of Europa and Ganymede; https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/jupiter-moons/io/ (accessed 2026-10-18)
Peale, S. J., Cassen, P. and Reynolds, R. T. 1979, Melting of Io by Tidal Dissipation, Science 203, 892-894, doi 10.1126/science.203.4383.892
Morabito, L. A. 2012, Discovery of Volcanic Activity on Io: A Historical Review, arXiv 1211.2554

panels.title: Four laps, two laps, one lap
body: Io has two big neighbours farther out, Europa and Ganymede. In about a week, Io circles Jupiter four times, Europa twice and Ganymede once, and then the pattern repeats.
This steady beat keeps tugging Io's path out of round, so the squeezing never stops. You can watch Europa and Ganymede keep the beat in this scene.
details: Orbital periods: Io 1.769 days (about 42.5 hours), Europa 3.551 days, Ganymede 7.155 days (NASA fact sheet). Four Io orbits take 7.08 days and two Europa orbits 7.10 days.
This moment is seven days after the scene starts: in that week Io has gone round Jupiter about four times. The moons' positions in this scene come from NASA JPL's Horizons system.
sources: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Jovian Satellite Fact Sheet: orbital periods Io 1.769138 d, Europa 3.551181 d, Ganymede 7.154553 d; https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/joviansatfact.html (accessed 2026-10-18)
NASA Science, Io: the precisely timed pulls of Europa and Ganymede; https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/jupiter-moons/io/ (accessed 2026-10-18)
Peale, S. J., Cassen, P. and Reynolds, R. T. 1979, Melting of Io by Tidal Dissipation, Science 203, 892-894: the resonance with Europa and Ganymede keeps Io's orbit eccentric

families.label: The big four (Galilean moons)
families.description: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto: the four large moons, all discovered in 1610. Each has a Planetary Explorer body package.

families.label: Inner moons (Amalthea group)
families.description: Metis, Adrastea, Amalthea and Thebe: small regular moons inside Io's orbit, on nearly circular orbits close to Jupiter.

families.label: Himalia group
families.description: Irregular moons on similar prograde orbits about 11 to 12 million km out, taken to be pieces of one parent body.

families.label: Ananke group
families.description: Irregular moons on similar retrograde orbits about 20 to 22 million km out, taken to be pieces of one parent body.

families.label: Carme group
families.description: Irregular moons on similar retrograde orbits about 22 to 24 million km out, taken to be pieces of one parent body.

families.label: Pasiphae group
families.description: Irregular moons on retrograde orbits with a wide spread of distances and shapes; Sinope is listed here though it may have been captured separately.

families.label: Carpo group
families.description: Two small prograde irregular moons on orbits further out than the Himalia group (Carpo and S/2018 J 4).

families.label: Loners
families.description: Moons in no published family: Themisto (prograde, the innermost irregular) and Valetudo (prograde, on an orbit that crosses the retrograde moons').

features.name: Pele
features.description: Pele is one of Io's signature active volcanoes, famous for the enormous red-orange deposit surrounding its vent. Its umbrella-shaped sulphur dioxide plume can rise hundreds of kilometres above the surface, while fresh sulphur-rich fallout continually repaints the surrounding plains.

details.label: Plume height
details.value: Up to about 300 km

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Large red-orange ring deposit near the anti-Jovian hemisphere

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pele's red deposits are made from unstable sulphur compounds, so the colour fades unless new eruptions keep refreshing it.

features.name: Loki Patera
features.description: Loki Patera is Io's most powerful volcanic feature by heat output: a huge, dark, horseshoe-shaped lava lake more than 200 km across. Its surface appears to overturn in waves as a cooling crust founders and exposes fresh molten rock beneath.

details.label: Size
details.value: Roughly 200 km across

details.label: Activity pattern
details.value: Large brightenings have been observed on roughly year-scale cycles

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: At peak activity, Loki can dominate Io's infrared brightness, making it observable from large Earth-based telescopes.

features.name: Prometheus
features.description: Prometheus is one of Io's most reliable plume sources, active in Voyager, Galileo, and later observations. Lava flows interact with sulphur dioxide frost, driving a bright plume that lays down a pale circular deposit around the vent region.

details.label: Plume height
details.value: About 75-100 km

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Bright plume deposit around a dark lava flow field

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Prometheus has been active for decades, making it one of the Solar System's longest-monitored active eruptions.

features.name: Tvashtar Paterae
features.description: Tvashtar Paterae sits in Io's high northern latitudes and is known for some of the most dramatic volcanic images ever returned. Galileo saw a glowing curtain of lava here, and New Horizons later caught a towering plume backlit by the Sun.

details.label: Lava curtain
details.value: More than 25 km long in Galileo observations

details.label: Plume height
details.value: About 330 km in New Horizons imagery

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tvashtar's backlit plume looked like a blue-white fountain arcing above Io's limb during the 2007 New Horizons flyby.

features.name: Ra Patera
features.description: Ra Patera is surrounded by sweeping, multi-coloured lava and sulphur flows that radiate outward from the caldera. Changes between Voyager and Galileo images made it a textbook example of how quickly Io's surface can be resurfaced.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Radiating yellow, orange, and brown flow patterns

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The colours around Ra Patera trace different sulphur compounds and temperatures, turning the landscape into a volcanic chemistry map.

features.name: Emakong Patera
features.description: Emakong Patera is bordered by long, bright deposits that contrast strongly with Io's darker volcanic terrain. The light-toned material is interpreted as sulphur dioxide frost or sulphur-rich flows, showing that Io's eruptions are not all the same composition.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Bright white-yellow flow deposits west of the vent region

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Io's surface chemistry is constantly recycled: volcanic gases freeze out, are altered by radiation, then are buried or blasted away by later eruptions.

features.name: Amirani
features.description: Amirani hosts one of the largest active lava flow fields known anywhere, stretching for hundreds of kilometres across Io. Galileo images showed new lava breakouts appearing along the margins, documenting resurfacing almost in real time.

details.label: Flow field
details.value: Hundreds of kilometres long

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Io is resurfaced so rapidly that impact craters, common on most solid worlds, are essentially absent.

features.name: Hi'iaka Patera
features.description: Hi'iaka Patera is a dark volcanic center set against bright sulphur dioxide plains. The sharp contrast between dark silicate lava and pale frost makes this region a useful guide to Io's repeated cycle of eruption, fallout, and resurfacing.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Dark lava patches on brighter yellow-white plains

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Dark flows on Io are usually fresh, hot silicate lava; bright areas are often frost or sulphur-rich deposits laid down by plumes.

features.name: Pillan Patera
features.description: Pillan Patera produced one of the largest eruptions directly witnessed by spacecraft. In 1997, Galileo observed a new dark pyroclastic deposit spreading across the surface, evidence of a powerful eruption that dramatically altered Io over months.

details.label: Eruption highlight
details.value: Major 1997 outburst seen by Galileo

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Dark deposit near Pele's red ring region

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pillan's eruption changed the visible surface so much that it became a natural before-and-after experiment for planetary volcanology.

features.name: Dazhbog Patera
features.description: Dazhbog Patera is a high-latitude volcanic depression in Io's northern hemisphere. It helps show that Io's heat flow is global: major volcanic centers are not confined to the equator, but appear across many latitudes.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Northern dark volcanic center

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Io's volcanoes are powered by tidal flexing from Jupiter and orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede, not by leftover formation heat alone.

features.name: Masubi Fluctus
features.description: Masubi Fluctus is a long lava-flow complex associated with repeated plume activity. Its flows and deposits trace how eruptions can migrate across Io's surface, burying older terrain under fresh volcanic material.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Fluctus: a named flow field

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Masubi's changing plume location suggests lava can travel far from its source before interacting with surface frost and launching gas into space.

features.name: Zamama
features.description: Zamama is an active volcanic center marked by a dark flow field and plume deposits. It represents Io's smaller but persistent volcanic systems: less famous than Loki or Pele, yet part of the dense network that keeps the whole moon geologically young.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Dark flow field with nearby pale plume deposits

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Hundreds of volcanic centers are known or suspected on Io, making it the most volcanically active world in the Solar System.

sources: Place names, kinds, descriptions and coordinates: Planetary Explorer's feature lists
Map pictures: USGS Astrogeology and NASA mission mosaics
provenance.accuracy: Each place is drawn where it was checked against the map picture by eye, not at a surveyed position; a marker can sit a few degrees from the feature's centre, and a polar entry is a representative anchor, not a feature centre.
provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

features.name: Conamara Chaos
features.description: Conamara Chaos is Europa's showcase example of disrupted ice. Blocks of older crust appear to have broken apart, rotated, drifted, and refrozen in a darker matrix, giving scientists a rare look at how warm ice or shallow liquid water can remodel the surface.

details.label: Approximate extent
details.value: About 800 by 400 km

details.label: Science value
details.value: A key analogue for possible exchange between Europa's surface and ocean-bearing interior

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright rafts embedded in darker, mottled terrain near low northern latitudes

features.name: Murias Chaos
features.description: Murias Chaos, nicknamed the Mitten, is an elevated chaos terrain on Europa's leading hemisphere. Unlike the classic broken-raft look of Conamara Chaos, Murias is often interpreted as the surface expression of a large warm-ice diapir that rose through the shell, breached the surface, and spread material outward.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: About 116 by 77 km

details.label: Nickname
details.value: The Mitten, named for its distinctive outline

details.label: Science value
details.value: A rare example used to test whether some chaos terrain forms by diapiric uplift and cryovolcanic extrusion

features.name: Thera Macula
features.description: Thera Macula is a dark, irregular patch in Europa's southern hemisphere. It is commonly interpreted as young chaos terrain where warm material rose through the ice shell, thinning or breaking the surface and leaving behind a chemically distinct deposit.

details.label: Why it matters
details.value: Often discussed as a candidate place where ocean-derived material may have reached shallow depths

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dark southern feature close to Thrace Macula and Cyclades Macula

features.name: Thrace Macula
features.description: Thrace Macula is one of the dark reddish spots that interrupt Europa's bright icy plains. Its colour and texture point to contaminated ice, salts, or hydrated materials concentrated where the crust has been disturbed.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Macula: a dark spot or patch on an icy world

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dark patch paired with nearby Thera Macula in the southern hemisphere

features.name: Cyclades Macula
features.description: Cyclades Macula is a named dark patch in Europa's high southern latitudes. It helps show that Europa's surface chemistry and thermal history vary strongly from place to place rather than forming a uniform ice shell.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 107 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: IAU Gazetteer center latitude and west longitude

features.name: Castalia Macula
features.description: Castalia Macula is a broad, dark, young-looking depression on Europa. Studies of this region connect its mottled texture to local resurfacing, collapse, and the movement of warm or briny material within the ice shell.

details.label: Nickname
details.value: Often described as one of Europa's dark spots

details.label: Science value
details.value: Useful for comparing collapse-style terrain with blocky chaos terrain

features.name: Agave Linea
features.description: Agave Linea is a long ridge-and-trough belt formed as Europa's brittle ice cracked under Jupiter-driven tidal stress. Dark material along the fracture likely includes salts or non-ice contaminants brought upward and altered by radiation.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Linea: an elongated bright or dark marking, ridge, or fracture system

details.label: What it records
details.value: Repeated opening, shear, and refreezing in Europa's mobile ice shell

features.name: Argo Linea
features.description: Argo Linea is one of Europa's long, dark lineaments. Its scale and continuity make it a useful guide to the global stress fields that have fractured Europa's surface through time.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Long dark band crossing brighter icy plains

details.label: Earth analogue
details.value: Some Europan double ridges are compared with refrozen cracks and meltwater features in terrestrial ice sheets

features.name: Belus Linea
features.description: Belus Linea is a dark triple-band feature imaged by Galileo. Bands like this are among Europa's most distinctive landforms: paired margins and a central bright stripe suggest repeated cracking, widening, and infilling by material from below.

details.label: Formation clue
details.value: Diffuse dark margins may record erupted or intruded debris along the crack

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dark banding near the anti-Jovian hemisphere

features.name: Cadmus Linea
features.description: Cadmus Linea is part of Europa's dense network of named ridges and bands. Its position among crossing lineae shows how Europa's surface preserves multiple generations of stress, extension, and resurfacing.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Low-latitude banding amid brighter icy plains

features.name: Rhadamanthys Linea
features.description: Rhadamanthys Linea is a prominent named fracture system on Europa. It belongs to the world-spanning pattern of ridges and bands that reveal an ice shell continually stressed by orbital resonance with Io and Ganymede.

details.label: Orbital link
details.value: Europa's 2:1 resonance with Io keeps its orbit slightly eccentric, sustaining tidal flexing

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Elongated ridge system west of the central anti-Jovian terrain

features.name: Tyre
features.description: Tyre is a large multi-ring impact structure and one of Europa's clearest examples of a major impact into an icy shell. Its concentric rings are interpreted as the crust's response to impact energy moving through ice over a warmer, weaker layer.

details.label: Diameter

details.label: Why craters are rare

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright circular ring structure in the northern hemisphere

features.name: Pwyll
features.description: Pwyll is Europa's freshest and most visually striking crater. Bright rays of excavated ice stretch far from the impact site, crossing older ridges and plains and making the crater easy to identify on global maps.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 26 km

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Bright ray system radiating across darker lineated terrain

details.label: Science value
details.value: Fresh ejecta exposes cleaner ice from below Europa's radiation-darkened surface

features.name: Cilix
features.description: Cilix is a small, well-preserved impact crater near Europa's equator. It is especially important for mapping because the longitude of its center defines Europa's longitude system, anchoring the 0-360 degree west-longitude convention used by the global texture.

details.label: Diameter

details.label: Mapping role

details.value: Galileo stereo imaging shows raised rims, wall slumping, and a central massif on the crater floor

features.name: Manannan
features.description: Manannan is a young impact crater whose ejecta and disturbed surroundings provide a window into Europa's near-surface structure. Like Pwyll, it is valuable because fresh impacts excavate material before radiation can fully alter it.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Simple impact crater with surrounding ejecta

details.label: Science value
details.value: Fresh impact material helps constrain the composition and strength of Europa's upper ice shell

features.name: Tara Regio
features.description: Tara Regio is a geologically complex region that includes reddish, disrupted terrain and lineaments. Spectral studies have linked parts of this area with salts or altered ocean-derived materials concentrated on the trailing hemisphere.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Regio: a broad named region with distinct appearance

details.label: Science value
details.value: Candidate area for studying non-ice materials on Europa's surface

features.name: Powys Regio
features.description: Powys Regio marks a broad province of mottled and lineated terrain. Large regions like this help connect local landforms to Europa-wide resurfacing patterns and to the changing stress field of the rotating ice shell.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Broad southern terrain province cut by many lineae

details.label: Interpretation
details.value: A regional record of older plains being overprinted by younger fractures and bands

features.name: North Polar Region
features.description: Europa's north polar terrain receives intense bombardment from particles trapped in Jupiter's magnetosphere. Radiation changes surface ice chemistry, creating oxidants and reddish contaminants that may eventually be cycled downward.

details.label: Environment
details.value: Strong radiation processing from Jupiter's magnetosphere

details.label: Astrobiology link
details.value: Surface oxidants could become chemical energy sources if transported into the ocean

features.name: South Polar Region
features.description: Europa's south polar region is important because possible water-vapour plumes have been reported there in Hubble observations. If active plumes exist, they could offer a way to sample ocean-related material without landing.

details.label: Observation note
details.value: Plume detections remain challenging and have not been continuously confirmed

details.label: Mission value
details.value: A plume fly-through could sample material sourced from Europa's ice shell or ocean

features.name: Galileo Regio
features.description: Galileo Regio is Ganymede's largest named dark terrain province and one of the oldest recognizable surfaces in the Solar System. Its dense impact record preserves crust that survived before later tectonic extension broke much of Ganymede into younger bright grooved terrain.

features.name: Uruk Sulcus

features.name: Mashu Sulcus

features.name: Gilgamesh

features.name: Osiris

features.name: Lakhmu Fossae

features.name: Anshar Sulcus

features.name: Dardanus Sulcus

features.name: Mysia Sulci

features.name: Barnard Regio

features.name: Marius Regio

features.name: North Polar Cap
features.description: Ganymede's north polar region is brightened by water frost and shaped by charged particles moving through Jupiter's magnetosphere. features.name: South Polar Cap

details.label: Map cue

details.label: Science value
details.value: A natural endpoint for explaining why Ganymede is both an icy world and a magnetized world.

features.name: Valhalla

features.name: Svol Catena
features.description: Svol Catena is a low northern crater chain near the Valhalla side of Callisto. Together with Gipul and Gomul, it makes crater chains easier to compare against large ringed structures in the same broad hemisphere.

features.name: North Polar Region
features.description: Callisto's north polar region is a densely cratered ancient landscape that has remained largely geologically quiet for billions of years. Unlike Io, Europa, and Ganymede, Callisto is not locked in the same strong orbital resonance, so Jupiter's tides have not continually refreshed its surface.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: High northern cratered terrain above 80 degrees north

details.label: Why it matters
details.value: The polar regions help show that Callisto's old impact record is global, not limited to the famous basin hemisphere.

details.label: Exploration note
details.value: Callisto's distance from Jupiter keeps it outside the most intense radiation zones around the planet.

features.name: South Polar Region
features.description: Callisto's south polar region continues the moon's ancient cratered character into high southern latitudes. Its terrain is a reminder that Callisto is a fossilized record of early outer Solar System bombardment, with far less resurfacing than the inner Galilean moons.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: High southern cratered terrain below 80 degrees south

details.label: Exploration note
details.value: Callisto has been discussed as a potential future staging point because it offers solid terrain with a much lower radiation burden than Io or Europa.

details.label: Science value
details.value: Comparing both poles with Valhalla and Asgard helps separate global crater saturation from local basin structure.
